paras: The hanging of Gibbs and Coleman was a night attack at Hickman, Kentucky, around 1 January 1881, in which a band hung two Black men suspected of arson to a tree until they were nearly dead. Both survived, and Black residents sought federal protection and warrants against what the Hickman Courier called a "ku klux squad."
Hickman had had a fire, a safe explosion and a robbery, "shrouded in considerable mystery," and suspicion "ran pretty strong against Gibbs and Coleman with some."

On a Saturday night, apparently 1 January, the attackers took the men from their beds and, according to a wire brief, hung them "until they were nearly dead, and then cut them down." The Courier implied the aim was a confession, hoping for proof "without the necessity of forcing a confession." The wire counted "a dozen respectable citizens"; Black residents told the Courier there were seven.

On Monday, Black residents telegraphed the United States Marshal for protection, and he directed them to a magistrate. On Tuesday they asked Judge Bailey for warrants against two suspected members but decided not to file affidavits "for the present." The Courier expected the matter to wait for the February Circuit Court term; no later report of warrants or a trial was found. Most townspeople, the Courier wrote, were "satisfied of their innocence"; the wire said the men had proven it.

On 5 January the Omaha Daily Bee ran an "Electric Briefs" item calling the attackers "respectable citizens" and then the men's "persecutors." The Courier's item of 7 January, "Getting After the Ku Klux," called the act "ku kluxing" but mostly defended local magistrates as "ready and willing to do their duty."

In March the Courier reprinted a sketch of Hickman by the editor of the Ohio Falls Express, "a colored man's paper," which ranged the town "from a safe-blower to a wagon factory" and its kindness from "an impartial magistrate to the Ku-Klux Klan."
The wire said the men "have had their persecutors arrested." The Courier, local and two days later, said no affidavits had been filed, so no warrants had issued.

reader.title: Hanging of Gibbs and Coleman at Hickman
bases: A band hanged two Black men suspected of arson or of the fire and robbery at Hickman until they were nearly dead and then cut them down; no death is reported (A2, A3).

A 'ku klux squad' of seven, or a dozen men, hanged the two suspects without authority on an accusation of arson (A2, A3), but the wire report says they were cut down 'nearly dead' and later proved their innocence, so no one was killed (A2).
An Omaha wire brief and the local Hickman Courier independently report the night hanging of two Black men suspected over the fire (A2, A3); they differ on the number of men and on arrests.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A dozen 'respectable citizens' took two Black men accused of arson from their beds and hung them to a tree until nearly dead; the men proved their innocence and had their persecutors arrested.

accounts.label: Local paper (Hickman Courier)
accounts.gist: A 'ku klux squad' hanged Gibbs and Coleman on Saturday night; Black residents sought federal protection and warrants, but no affidavits were sworn, and the paper thought most townspeople now believed the men innocent.

accounts.label: Black residents' claim (via the Courier)
accounts.gist: Seven men made up the squad, and witnesses could identify two of them.

framing.detail: A one-sentence-pair brief in the Bee's 'Electric Briefs' column, calling the attackers 'respectable citizens' and later 'persecutors' and stating the men's innocence.
The Courier's 'Getting After the Ku Klux' named the act 'ku kluxing' and leaned toward the men's innocence, but chiefly defended local magistrates and said US officials 'could do no more'.

conflicts.note: The Courier's figure comes from the victims' side; the wire's is unattributed.

versions.value: warrants sought for two suspects, but no affidavits filed and no warrants issued

conflicts.note: The Courier is local, detailed and dated two days later; its account of the warrant application is the better evidence for the first week.

quotes: A dozen respectable citizens of Hickman, Ky., went to the homes of two negroes accused of arson, took them from their beds, and hung them to tree until they were nearly dead, and then cut them down.
The negroes have proven their innocence of the crime they were accused of, and have had their persecutors arrested.
